raw_text:
### Introduction and Epidemiology
Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) represents an underdiagnosed but increasingly recognized cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy and progressive heart failure (HF) [1]. Historically considered a rare disease, recent epidemiologic data, driven by improvements in noninvasive imaging, demonstrate that cardiac amyloid deposition is a relatively common cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and severe aortic stenosis, particularly in elderly populations [2,3]. There are two main types of amyloid proteins that clinically manifest as CA: light chain amyloidosis (AL) and transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR) [3]. ATTR is further classified into wild-type ATTR (wtATTR), a non-genetic senile form, and hereditary ATTR (hATTR), which is autosomal dominant and results from over 120 known pathogenic mutations in the transthyretin (*TTR*) gene [3].

### Pathophysiology and Classification
The core pathophysiology of CA involves the misfolding of precursor proteins into unstable monomeric intermediates that aggregate to form insoluble beta-pleated sheet amyloid fibrils, which are subsequently deposited in the extracellular space of the myocardium [4]. According to the International Society of Amyloidosis nomenclature committee, more than 30 amyloidogenic proteins exist in humans [5]. In AL amyloidosis, a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia overproduces monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains that possess direct cardiotoxic properties, causing rapid tissue damage alongside physical infiltration [4]. Conversely, ATTR is characterized by the destabilization of the homotetrameric TTR protein synthesized by the liver, leading to dissociation into monomeric forms, subsequent misfolding, and slow extracellular deposition in myocardial and tenosynovial tissues [6].

### Clinical Presentation
CA typically manifests as a progressive restrictive cardiomyopathy with severe diastolic dysfunction, leading to HF with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction [7]. Patients frequently present with dyspnea, fatigue, orthostatic hypotension, and atrial arrhythmias [2]. Classic "red flag" clinical findings include extracardiac manifestations that precede cardiac symptoms by several years [3]. Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, and biceps tendon rupture are highly specific tenosynovial clues for underlying wtATTR [8]. Prospective screening studies indicate that up to 5% of patients over age 60 undergoing bilateral carpal tunnel surgery are subsequently diagnosed with CA [9].

### Diagnostic Evaluation
Initial assessment usually begins with standard electrocardiography (ECG) and transthoracic echocardiography (TTE). Low QRS voltage on ECG relative to the degree of left ventricular (LV) wall thickness is a classic indicator, although normal or high voltage (suggesting hypertrophy) is still observed in a substantial proportion of patients [10]. TTE typically demonstrates concentric myocardial thickening, biatrial enlargement, and interatrial septal thickening [2]. The most specific echocardiographic sign is relative apical sparing of global longitudinal strain (GLS), characterized by preserved longitudinal contraction at the apex and markedly reduced strain at the base [11,12].

Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging provides a more comprehensive evaluation, exhibiting a characteristic global subendocardial pattern of late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) and abnormal gadolinium kinetics [13]. T1 mapping and extracellular volume (ECV) quantification on CMR are sensitive tools for evaluating early amyloid deposition and estimating the systemic amyloid burden, which directly correlates with clinical prognosis [14].

An accurate diagnosis requires differentiating AL from ATTR CA, as their clinical courses and treatments diverge significantly [15]. Initial screening must rule out monoclonal light chains using serum free light chain (FLC) assays and serum/urine immunofixation electrophoresis (SIFE/UIFE) [16]. Bone-seeking radiotracers, such as technetium-99m pyrophosphate ($^{99\text{m}}$Tc-PYP) or $^{99\text{m}}$Tc-diphosphonopropanedicarboxylic acid ($^{99\text{m}}$Tc-DPD), have revolutionized the diagnostic paradigm [17,18]. Visual myocardial tracer uptake of Perugini grade 2 or 3 in the absolute absence of a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia achieves a positive predictive value of nearly 100% for ATTR CA, completely eliminating the historical necessity of an endomyocardial biopsy for these patients [19,20]. However, if monoclonal light chains are detected or if imaging remains equivocal, tissue biopsy (such as endomyocardial or abdominal fat pad biopsy) with Congo red staining showing apple-green birefringence remains the gold standard for definitive diagnostic confirmation [21,22].

### Therapeutic Strategies
The therapeutic approach to cardiac amyloidosis involves treating the underlying etiology and managing heart failure symptoms. Traditional HF therapies like beta-blockers, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, and calcium channel blockers are often poorly tolerated or contraindicated in CA due to the restrictive physiology and dependence on heart rate to maintain cardiac output; instead, loop diuretics and aldosterone antagonists are the mainstay of volume management [2].

For AL amyloidosis, therapy is directed at suppressing the underlying clonal plasma cell dyscrasia [23]. The standard upfront treatment has traditionally been a combination of cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone (CyBorD) [24]. However, the landmark ANDROMEDA trial established that adding the anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody daratumumab to CyBorD significantly accelerates and deepens hematologic response, improving organ survival and overall prognosis [25].

For ATTR amyloidosis, treatment aims to either stabilize the TTR tetramer or silence its hepatic production. Tafamidis, a small-molecule TTR stabilizer, was shown in the pivotal ATTR-ACT trial to significantly reduce all-cause mortality and cardiovascular-related hospitalizations in both wtATTR and hATTR patients [26]. Acoramidis, a novel high-affinity TTR stabilizer, has similarly demonstrated strong efficacy and safety, with robust reductions in clinical events over 30 months of treatment [27]. Alternatively, gene-silencing therapies, which employ RNA interference (RNAi) or antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), halt hepatic TTR synthesis. Patisiran (an RNAi agent) and inotersen (an ASO) have been established as highly effective treatments for hATTR-associated polyneuropathy [28,29]. More recently, the subcutaneously administered RNAi therapeutic vutrisiran was shown in the HELIOS-B trial to significantly lower all-cause mortality and recurrent cardiovascular events in patients with ATTR cardiomyopathy [30].

### Conclusion
The clinical landscape of cardiac amyloidosis has undergone a profound paradigm shift. Transitioning from a disease characterized by delayed diagnosis and lack of treatment options, modern medicine now relies on highly sensitive noninvasive diagnostic algorithms and a rapidly expanding toolkit of targeted, disease-modifying therapies that have substantially improved survival and quality of life.
